author: KTOOpubmedia
title: Why are Juneau's highest-paid city employees mostly cops?
text: Why are Juneau’s highest-paid city employees mostly cops? Police leadership said the wage data underscores the department’s years-long struggle to fill vacant positions, which means some officers have been clocking in more and more overtime. But that comes with its own trade-offs. Juneau’s highest-paid city employee in 2025 was a cop. So was the second highest. And the third. In fact, 6 out of the 10 top-paid city employees last year were officers at the Juneau Police Department. That’s according to a records request by KTOO to the City and Borough of Juneau. Last year, Juneau’s top earner was Police Sgt. Michael Wise. He made just over $272,000 in gross earnings.By comparison, the city’s top administrator — the city manager — earned about $230,000. The police chief, Derek Bos, earned $191,000. He wasn’t in the top 10. Police leadership said the data underscores the department’s years-long struggle to fill vacant positions.Right now, the department is short 10 officers. To fill that gap, some officers have been clocking in more and more overtime. But that comes with its own trade-offs — thewarns that long shifts and extensive overtime can degrade an officer’s decision-making ability, creating safety risks for the community and the officers.Juneau’s top paid city employees in terms of gross earnings in 2025 were Police Sergeants Michael Wise and Brian Dallas, and Police Officer Terry Allen, according to the data. Wise ranked at the top with gross earnings of about $272,000 in 2025 — which breaks down to nearly $23,000 a month. Dallas made $260,000 and Allen made $230,000. A lot of that is made up of overtime pay, which the police chief and city manager aren’t eligible for.In 2025, Wise, Dallas and Allen were paid a baseline rate of between $63 and $72 an hour, and worked between 629 and 1,050 hours of overtime. All three officers declined an interview with KTOO. The amount an officer gets paid working overtime is determined by a formula in the police union’s contract with the city.Generally, it’s aboutOfficer Allen clocked the most overtime, topping out with more than 1,000 hours — which averages to roughly 20 extra hours every week beyond his regular job.citing the potentially dangerous consequences of fatigue and long shifts, paying for overtime has become a growing piece of the Juneau Police Department’s budget. According to data, the department has spent more on overtime pay every year for at least the past five years.Between fiscal year 2021 and 2025, JPD spent a total of $6.5 million in overtime pay, which is roughly $2.3 million more than what was originally budgeted. Despite that extra overtime pay, data shows the department’s spending as a whole each year was actually below budget. That’s largely because of its high number of staff vacancies — when positions go unfilled, the city saves money on those salaries.It’s common to see police officers working large amounts of overtime and ranking at the top of their city’s pay charts. Larger cities in the U.S. likealso have officers pulling in six-figure incomes, most commonly because of overtime work due to short staffing. Like Juneau, those communities are also grappling with having enough officers on duty and the safety issues that could rise from overworking those officers.In an interview with KTOO, Juneau Police Chief Derek Bos said overtime work has become essential for the department, especially in recent years.“We’re in this catch-22 where we have to cover shifts, which means there has to be overtime that people work, but we still have to care for everybody who’s working that much,” he said. “Not showing up is not an option. ” Juneau Police Chief Derek Bos speaks during a press briefing on Tuesday, Aug. 12, 2025. But Bos contends that the department, which currently has 45 officers, doesn’t demand mandatory overtime, at least not right now. Instead, officers usually sign up voluntarily. And some more than others.“There is nothing that says we expect them to work 90 hours or 91 hours or 93 and a half hours,” he said. “The expectation is that those shifts get covered, but there’s discretion on who signs up for those and how that works. ” Bos said short staffing for both officers and dispatchers has unfortunately become a norm at the department despite robust efforts to recruit new members.A few years ago, the department lowered the minimum number of officers required to be on patrol.“We track how much they’re working, how much is too much, and sometimes that comes down to the individual. It comes down to what they’re doing,” he said. He said the department is constantly trying to address burnout and fatigue. But it’s a balancing act with the responsibilities the department has to the community.“We are there 365 days a year, 24 hours a day. It would not be okay for us to say we’re only going to work 16 hours a day, because then what happens the other eight hours of the day? So, not being there is not really an option,” he said. Juneau Police Sgt.Sterling Salisbury is the chapter president for the Public Safety Employees Association, the union that represents the majority of JPD staff. In an interview with KTOO, he said the overtime data doesn’t surprise him, and he worries some officers are nearing their breaking point. When asked about safety issues with overworked officers, Salisbury said staffing shortages can make policing much more stressful.“When you’re at that minimum staffing or very close to minimum staffing, you’re pretty reactive,” he said. “You’re not super proactive, just because you’re constantly trying to play catch up. ” Juneau Police Department Officer Terry Allen talks into a radio while on patrol duty in downtown Juneau on Monday, Sept. 9, 2024. Salisbury said the union has tried for years to get a contract that makes Juneau’s department stand out among other agencies in Alaska.The union negotiates in the hopes that it will attract new people to fill prolonged vacancies.“If you want to beat those competitors, you have to look more attractive — that’s really what it boils down to,” he said. But Salisbury said it’s been difficult. This past contract negotiation cycle, it took a year for the union and city to negotiate a contract, and it required arbitration. While JPD pays entry-level offers more than many other departments in the state, Salisbury said it still doesn’t seem to be moving the needle.Salisbury said offering Juneau officers more money isn’t the only solution to fixing the department’s chronic vacancies, but it definitely wouldn’t hurt.“I always tell people, ‘Well, if you paid someone $500 an hour, we would be staffed next week. If you paid someone $5 an hour, we would have no staff. ’ And so you have to find that middle ground of what can the city afford, what is needed and what’s realistic,” he said.The city has its own money issues right now, says Mayor Beth Weldon.to close one city facility, reduce funding to some services and dip into its reserves to patch a multimillion-dollar recurring budget hole. ThisWeldon said the city does its best to make its pay competitive with other agencies across the state. But she said they also have to be realistic with its budget restraints.“There is no clean solution — wish there was — but there’s no clean solution,” she said. “All we can do is keep trying to be the best employer in the city. ” She said there are several factors that make Juneau a more difficult place to recruit employees in general, not just police. On top of that,“People just don’t want to be police officers like they used to,” Weldon said.“I mean, how many kids this day and age do you know that say they want to be a police officer when they grow up? Very few. ”
